# The impact of resolution and flipping on image classification

# Yinuo Zhang

Lappeenranta–Lahti University of Technology,Lahti,15210,Finland.

2643787985@qq.com

Abstract. The initial stage of image classification involves image preprocessing, which includes considerations such as the object's position within the image, the background, ambient lighting, and the viewing angle. These factors can introduce variations in the original pixel data, and consequently, applying diverse preprocessing methods can yield varying levels of accuracy in the collected data. This study explores the relationship between preprocessing techniques and the performance of deep learning models. In this paper, images are processed by both reducing and increasing their resolution and by applying 180° horizontal and vertical flips. Subsequently, the Edge Impulse platform (https://edgeimpulse.com/) is employed for image classification. The objective of this paper is to assess the impact of resolution adjustments and flipping on image classification accuracy through a series of repeated experimental analyses.

Keywords: Image classification, Edge impulse, Image flipping, Reduced resolution.

## 1. Introduction

In contemporary society, image processing holds significant relevance, and image classification serves as the cornerstone for a wide array of image processing tasks. With the proliferation of mobile internet, the prevalence of smartphones, and the omnipresence of social media, there has been an exponential surge in image and video data. Concurrently, technology has wielded a profound influence on human life, particularly in realms such as work and entertainment. Applications such as automatic object tracking, facial recognition, fingerprint identification, and image enhancement are just a few examples that hinge upon the accurate identification of elements within images or videos. For most video processing applications, the processing of individual video frames (images) is indispensable. Selecting specific processing techniques and model algorithms in accordance with distinct application requirements often proves to be imperative. Hence, the precise classification of objects within images assumes paramount importance for subsequent stages of image processing. Even the most advanced computer vision models can yield poor performance when fed with lowquality input data[7]. Hence, the quality of the data directly influences the accuracy of the outcomes. Even when working with high-quality images, preprocessing plays a pivotal role in achieving optimal experimental results. Image preprocessing constitutes the initial and crucial phase of image classification. Prior to commencing model training, image enhancement techniques can be employed to enhance image quality, including adjustments to size, resolution, color, and orientation. It's worth noting that the quality of the images can, to some extent, impact the duration and complexity of the training process. The breakthrough of the AlexNet model proposed by Alex Krizhevsky et al [8] in 2012 was an important turning point in the field of large-scale image classification. The network model dramatically outperformed traditional image classification methods, which was the first application of deep learning to large-scale image classification, and since then, a series of CNN models have emerged [15-19]. The introduction of the AlexNet model by Alex Krizhevsky et al. [8] in 2012 marked a significant milestone in the field of large-scale image classification. This pioneering neural network outperformed traditional image classification methods, representing the first successful application of deep learning to large-scale image classification. Since then, a series of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models have emerged, as documented in references [15-19]. In the AlexNet architecture, the initial layers utilized larger convolutional kernels, leading to a substantial increase in model parameters. VGGNet, proposed by Simonyan and Zisserman in 2015 [9], adopted a similar

## 2. Methods and Materials

The Edge Impulse platform serves as a comprehensive solution for creating datasets, conducting model training, optimizing library processes, and training image data for edge devices. Consequently, we selected it as the preferred platform for our image data training, result verification, and impact assessment. For this study, we utilized rice and mushroom datasets sourced from Kaggle [5] and a mushroom classification dataset [6]. We curated images of four distinct rice varieties and four different mushroom types for our research. Our goal is to provide valuable experimental data for professionals in this domain, aiding them in assessing the significance of image resolution and object perspectives in the image classification process and ultimately optimizing the results. Due to the substantial influence of image clarity and cropping on classification, we opted for rice microscope images. These images encompass four rice types: Arborio, Basmati, Ipsala, and Karacadag. Additionally, we conducted comparative studies on mushrooms, including four distinct classifications: Amanita, Boletus, Cortinarius, and Entoloma. We relied on Edge Impulse for data training during our experiments, utilizing 20 training cycles with a learning rate of 0.0005. Initially, we employed Python to randomly select and analyze 450 images from each rice type, totaling 1800 images. These images were uploaded to Edge Impulse for preliminary training and analysis, yielding initial training results. Subsequently, we horizontally flipped the 1800 images using Python and employed the same method for image classification training. Likewise, we vertically flipped 1800 images using Python and conducted preliminary data comparisons, drawing initial conclusions. In our experiments, the initial image (250 resolution) underwent a program-based resolution reduction to 100, followed by an increase to 350. To address the issue of limited preliminary test images and the resultant lower accuracy, we tested an additional 12,000 and 20,000 images. Furthermore, to evaluate the universality of resolution's impact on image classification, we included various types of mushroom images for testing. These tests were conducted under identical photo quality, photo quantity, and experimental methodologies. Our aim is to assess the generalizability of our experiment's results and to determine if outcomes vary with different photos. We aspire for our experiment to provide a practical exploration of analytical preprocessing for researchers in this field. Concurrently, the shift towards data-centric methods in research has prompted a transition from algorithm-centric to data-centric research. We hope that our research can offer practical guidance in this evolving landscape.

## 4. Analysis

### 4.1 The impact of flipping on image classification

In the experimental results, it was found that the microscope images of rice were relatively single and symmetrical. Compared with asymmetric animal and plant images, the results showed no significant upward or downward trend, thus indicating a more random pattern. This suggests that preprocessing data should not consider flipping, which could lead to an increase in loss and a reduction in model performance.

### 4.2 The impact of adjusting the resolution on image classification

Reducing image resolution has consistently shown substantial improvements in the performance of our classification model, as evidenced by multiple implementation results. Within our classification model, various indicators for image recognition and classification are at play, with resolution reduction emphasizing the structural features of rice grains. This reduction in pixel density corresponds to a significant decrease in the white space within rice images, leading to enhanced accuracy. This implies that, in certain rice models, structural features hold greater importance than other characteristics, such as color.Furthermore, previous research has observed that decreasing resolution in rice varieties with high recognition error rates mitigates specific losses. The classifier tends to exhibit elevated error rates due to the influence of other recognition factors. In support of this conclusion, we conducted an experiment involving the random selection of 20,000 images, where resolution was increased to 350. This revealed a notable decrease in accuracy, thus substantiating our findings. We hypothesize that simpler object images, characterized by relatively lower resolutions, offer more salient recognition features for the object, resulting in improved image classification outcomes. Conversely, complex images with higher resolutions and numerous recognition factors provide more reference points but dilute the significance of key factors in image classification. Consequently, this diminishes the accuracy of image recognition and classification. To enhance the accuracy of classifying such complex images, it may necessitate the development of more sophisticated classification model algorithms or the use of larger training image datasets.

### 4.3 The impact of changing resolution on rice classification

At the conclusion of the experiment, the study assessed the impact of changes in image resolution on the universality of the classification model, specifically in the context of mushroom classification. However, the results from the extended testing phase revealed an interesting pattern in contrast to rice classification. Increasing image resolution had a marginal positive effect on classification accuracy, while decreasing resolution led to a decline in accuracy. Although this observed trend did not reach statistical significance, it could be attributed to the complex background environments, diverse contributing factors to recognition, and variations in mushroom image colors. Consequently, it implies the need for additional factors to be incorporated

## 5. Conclusion and Future Work

This paper leverages Edge Impulse for the training and classification of rice images. It investigates the influence of resolution and image flipping on the results of image classification through a comprehensive data analysis. The findings reveal that flipping images has minimal to negligible impact on the accuracy of microscopic rice image classification. Conversely, image resolution exhibits an intriguing pattern. Lowering the image resolution increases presentation accuracy and reduces loss rates. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that rice images typically feature a uniform white background. In this dataset, decreasing resolution places greater emphasis on the rice's inherent features during automated classification, diminishing the influence of extraneous factors like color.However, it's noteworthy that the decrease in accuracy due to lower resolution is not consistently observed in mushroom classification datasets. We postulate that in cases featuring relatively cluttered images, lower resolution may indeed contribute to a reduction in accuracy, although this trend is not markedly pronounced. It's crucial to underscore that this study exclusively focused on the classification of rice and mushrooms, with no discernible implications for other types of image classification tasks. The results and implementations are specific to particular image datasets, such as those involving rice, and lack broad applicability. To attain more precise insights, future research endeavors should subject the classifier to a diverse array of datasets. Moreover, considering the limitations of the classifier, we recommend selecting a larger pool of images for multiple tests in subsequent studies. Beyond resolution and flipping, future research should delve into the impact of various other factors on automatic image classification. Simultaneously, the development of supplementary methods and techniques to enhance image contours will indirectly bolster the conclusions drawn from this study.

# Fucoidan improving spinal cord injury recovery: Modulating microenvironment and promoting remyelination

**Authors:** Haoming Shu; Xin Zhang; Yingyan Pu; Yinuo Zhang; Shixue Huang; Jun Ma; Li Cao; Xuhui Zhou

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Orthopedics, Second Affiliated Hospital, Naval Medical University, Shanghai, China | 2 Department of Neurobiology, Key Laboratory of Molecular Neurobiology of the Ministry of Education, Naval Medical University, Shanghai, China | 3 Department of Orthopedics, Shanghai General Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China

## Abstract

Excessive neuroinflammation, apoptosis, glial scar, and demyelination triggered by spinal cord injury (SCI) are major obstacles to SCI repair. Fucoidan, a natural marine plant extract, possesses broad‐spectrum anti‐inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects and is regarded as a potential therapeutic for various diseases, including neurological disorders. However, its role in SCI has not been investigated.

In this study, we established an SCI model in mice and intervened in injury repair by daily intraperitoneal injections of different doses of fucoidan (10 and 20 mg/kg). Concurrently, primary oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) were treated in vitro to validate the differentiation‐promoting effect of fucoidan on OPCs. Basso Mouse Scale (BMS), Louisville Swim Scale (LSS), and Rotarod test were carried out to measure the functional recovery. Immunofluorescence staining, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were performed to assess the neuroinflammation, apoptosis, glial scar, and remyelination. Western blot analysis was conducted to clarify the underlying mechanism of remyelination.

Our results indicate that in the SCI model, fucoidan exhibits significant anti‐inflammatory effects and promotes the transformation of pro‐inflammatory M1‐type microglia/macrophages into anti‐inflammatory M2‐type ones. Fucoidan enhances the survival of neurons and axons in the injury area and improves remyelination. Additionally, fucoidan promotes OPCs differentiation into mature oligodendrocytes by activating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway.

Fucoidan improves SCI repair by modulating the microenvironment and promoting remyelination.

Keywords: fucoidan, microenvironment, neuroinflammation, OPCs differentiation, remyelination, spinal cord injury

## Abstract

Our results indicate that in the SCI model, fucoidan exhibits significant anti‐inflammatory effects and promotes the transformation of pro‐inflammatory M1‐type microglia/macrophages into anti‐inflammatory M2‐type ones. Fucoidan enhances the survival of neurons and axons in the injury area and improves remyelination. Additionally, fucoidan promotes OPC differentiation into mature oligodendrocytes by activating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway. These findings suggest that fucoidan improves SCI repair by modulating the microenvironment and promoting remyelination.

## INTRODUCTION

Spinal cord injury (SCI) is devastating damage to the spinal cord, leading to serious dysfunction of sensation and locomotion and even death. The consequences that come with SCI include physical and mental damage, decreased quality of life, and a huge economic burden on society and patients with SCI. The SCI pathophysiological process is complex and considered to be initiated by the primary injury, followed by the secondary injury. 1 The primary injury is the mechanical force, commonly in the form of contusion or compression, acting on the spinal cord, resulting in blood–spinal cord barrier (BSCB) damage, nerve cell membrane disruption, and axon rupture. Secondary injury is the characteristic phase of SCI involving neuronal apoptosis, oxidative stress, demyelination, inflammation, and glial scar formation. 2 , 3 , 4 Extensive studies focusing on the damage factors have been performed but have shown limited therapeutic efficacy. 5

Following SCI, innate immune cells, including microglia, astrocytes, and endothelial cells, respond rapidly and release cytokines and chemokines. Classical inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin‐1 beta (IL‐1β), interleukin‐6 (IL‐6), and tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNF‐α), are upregulated within hours of SCI, leading to the assemblage of microglia and macrophages in the lesion core. 6 , 7 Furthermore, these assembled immune cells secrete additional pro‐inflammatory cytokines that result in exacerbation of inflammation. The cascade‐amplified inflammatory response produces many oxygen free radicals, destroys cells, triggers necrosis and apoptosis of nerve cells, exacerbates the formation of glial scars, and destroys the BSCB. 8 The aforementioned factors ultimately contribute to the formation of an inhibitory injury microenvironment and hinder the process of SCI recovery. 9 Additionally, demyelination, which commences shortly after SCI, has a detrimental impact on neural signal transmission and can cause axon disruption. 10 Therefore, promoting the survival, repair, and regeneration of the myelin sheath is crucial in the treatment of SCI.

Currently, therapeutic options for SCI are severely limited in scope. Methylprednisolone is widely used in clinical practice, but its dosage is positively correlated with the risk of complications such as gastrointestinal bleeding, hyperglycemia, and infection. 11 Aiming at developing effective and safe treatment methods for SCI, we screened for novel drugs that exhibit neuroprotective effects and promote myelin regeneration. Natural medicines have attracted our attention due to their low side effects. Fucoidan (Fuc) is a natural plant metabolite with highly attractive biological activities, such as anti‐inflammation, antioxidation, immunomodulation, and neuroprotection. 12 , 13 , 14

Fuc has been confirmed to exert a beneficial therapeutic role in several central nervous system diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, stroke, and brain injury. 15 , 16 In studies related to Alzheimer's disease, Fuc showed anti‐aggregation effects against amyloid fibrils and exert neuroprotection effects against Aβ‐induced neurotoxicity. 17 In a rotenone‐induced rat model of PD, chronic treatment with fucoidan significantly reversed the loss of nigral dopaminergic neurons by enhancing mitochondrial respiratory function. 15 Particularly, recent findings have indicated that Fuc could effectively protect neurons from transient global cerebral ischemia through attenuation of activated glial cells and reduction of oxidative stress by increasing superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity. 18 It has also been reported that Fuc has a significant protective effect on the progression of traumatic brain injury in mice. 19 However, it was still unclear whether fucoidan had beneficial effects in treating SCI.

In the present study, using a SCI mice model, we demonstrated that the administration of Fuc could suppress early inflammatory responses and, consequently, improve functional recovery following SCI and especially promote remyelination in the lesion region. In vitro experiments further demonstrated that this regenerative effect on myelin is associated with the role of Fuc in promoting OPCs differentiation and maturation through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. The findings shed light on re‐purposing Fuc to treat SCI.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Cells and cell culture

The isolation and purification of mouse primary OPCs/microglia were conducted according to established protocols with modifications tailored to our experimental setup. Briefly, cortical tissues from postnatal day 0 (P0) mice were dissected, homogenized, and cultured in poly‐D‐lysine‐coated T75 culture flasks containing DMEM/F12 supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) at 37°C in an atmosphere containing 5% CO2. The cultures were maintained for 10–12 days with regular medium changes every 3 days. The culture flasks were subjected to agitation at 180 rpm for 1 h and the medium was collected for primary microglia culture. The flasks was filled with fresh medium and shaken at 200 rpm for 18 h. Subsequently, the conditioned medium was collected and allowed to adhere to uncoated dishes for 40 min, promoting the attachment of microglia and astrocytes while preventing OPCs attachment. The resulting OPCs‐enriched suspension was then reseeded onto poly‐D‐lysine‐coated plates or coverslips at densities ranging from 5000 to 50,000 cells/cm2. For differentiation assays, OPCs were cultured in neurobasal medium supplemented with 2% B27 for 3 days prior to experimental analysis.

Primary cortical neurons were isolated from the cerebral cortex of P0 mice. Briefly, after the removal of blood vessels and meninges, the brain tissues were finely chopped into approximately 1 mm3 fragments and digested with 0.25% trypsin–EDTA and DNase I (MilliporeSigma) for 30 min. The digestion was terminated using 10% FBS, followed by centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 6 min. The cells were then seeded onto poly‐D‐lysine‐coated plates and incubated in neurobasal medium supplemented with 2% B27 and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. The culture medium was refreshed by replacing half of it every 2 days.

### Animals

Male C57/BL6 mice aged 8–9 weeks were procured from Shanghai Jihui Laboratory Animal Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China) for all animal experiments. Mice were housed under standardized conditions and maintained on a 12‐h light–dark cycle. All animal experiments were conducted following approval from the Animal Welfare and Research Ethics Committee of Shanghai Changzheng Hospital (Shanghai, China) and in strict accordance with the guidelines of the Chinese National Institutes of Health.

### SCI model

A crushed SCI model was performed as previously reported. 20 The animals were randomly assigned to one of three groups: vehicle, Fuc (10 mg/kg), and Fuc (20 mg/kg), with 20 animals per group. Anesthesia was induced using 3% inhaled isoflurane (Yaji Biological Technology, Shanghai, China) and maintained with 1.5% isoflurane. Subsequently, a laminectomy was performed at the T7‐9 level to expose the spinal cord. Spinal cord trauma was induced by laterally compressing the T8 spinal cord using a pair of forceps with a 0.40 mm spacer for 15 s.

### Immunofluorescence staining

For tissue samples, three mice per group were euthanized and transcardially perfused with PBS, followed by 4% paraformaldehyde solution at 8 weeks post‐injury. Spinal cord samples from the T11–12 region were harvested and post‐fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde solution for 12 h. Subsequently, the samples were dehydrated and embedded in OCT (Sakura) before being sectioned into 10 μm sections using a cryo‐ultramicrotome. Antigen retrieval was performed on sections using citrate buffer (0.01 M, pH 6).

For cell samples, cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min, followed by blocking with PBST blocking buffer containing 10% normal donkey serum. Primary antibodies, including anti‐MBP (1:200, MAB386, MilliporeSigma), anti‐caspase 3 (1:500, 9664, Cell Signaling Technology), anti‐NF200 (1:2000, ab207176, Abcam), anti‐CC1 (1:100, MABC200, MilliporeSigma), anti‐SOX10 (1:200, AF2864, R&D Systems), anti‐GFAP (1:500, ab7260, Abcam), anti‐NeuN (1:1000, ABN90, MilliporeSigma), anti‐Arg1 (1:50016001‐1‐AP, Proteintech), anti‐iNOS (1:500, 18985‐1‐AP, Proteintech), and anti‐CD68 (1:500, ab31630, Abcam) were incubated at 4°C overnight, followed by secondary antibodies (1:200, Jackson ImmunoResearch) at room temperature for 2 h. The sections were visualized using an Olympus IX70 microscope system (Olympus, Tokyo). Six randomly selected non‐overlapping fields from each section were analyzed for quantification.

### BrdU incorporation

To evaluate the proliferation of OPCs, 5‐bromo‐2‐deoxyuridine (BrdU, 10 μM; Sigma) was added to the culture medium 6 h prior to fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde solution. Subsequently, coverslips were incubated in 2 N HCl for 30 min, followed by treatment with 0.1 M borate buffer (pH 8.0) for 25 min to denature DNA. Permeabilization of OPCs was achieved using 0.2% Triton X‐100 for 2 min, followed by blocking with PBST containing 10% donkey serum for 1 h at room temperature. Coverslips were then incubated overnight with anti‐BrdU antibody (1:100, B35128, Invitrogen). After washing with PBS, cells were incubated with secondary antibodies (1:200, Jackson ImmunoResearch) and DAPI (Sigma) for 1 h at room temperature.

### TUNEL staining

In this experiment, tissue samples consisted of slices of spinal cord tissue harvested on day 7 post‐injury, while cell samples comprised OPCs subjected to a 3‐day differentiation period. Apoptotic cells were identified and quantified using a TUNEL Assay Kit (Beyotime), following the manufacturer's instructions. Additionally, the nuclei of all cells were counterstained with DAPI. Three sections were randomly selected from each group, and within each section, three fields of view were randomly chosen. The number of positive cells within these fields was then counted with ImageJ software (NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA).

### Live/dead staining

After 7 days of in vitro culture, the medium of primary cortical neurons was replaced with fresh medium containing hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, 100 μM, MilliporeSigma) for an additional 24 h. The cells were then randomly divided into four groups: a sham group (no H2O2 treatment), a vehicle control group (H2O2 treatment), and two Fuc groups (treated with H2O2 and Fuc at two concentrations).

Following the instructions provided in the live/dead staining kit (Solarbio Science & Technology), the culture medium was removed, and the cells were washed twice with 1× Assay Buffer for 2 min each. After adding Calcein‐AM staining solution, the cells were incubated at 37°C in the dark for 20 min. PI staining solution was then added, and the cells were stained in the dark at room temperature for 5 min. The staining solution was removed, and the cells were washed twice with 1× PBS for 2 min each. Finally, the slides were mounted and observed under a fluorescence microscope.

### Western blot analysis

Tissue and cell protein extraction reagents were used for total protein sample preparation. The protein concentration was determined using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Beyotime) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Equivalent quantities of protein samples were loaded and separated on sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide‐gel electrophoresis (SDS‐PAGE) at 140 V for approximately 90 min. Protein transfer from polyacrylamide gels to nitrocellulose (NC) membranes (Merck) was achieved by placing them together in an electrophoresis bath. Following protein transfer, membranes were blocked in 10% (w/v) milk at room temperature for 1 h, followed by overnight incubation with primary antibodies, including anti‐ARG1 (1:1000, 16001‐1‐AP, Proteintech), anti‐iNOS (1:1000, K0221, Santa Cruz), anti‐MBP (1:2000, AB7349, Abcam), anti‐p‐mTOR (1:1000, 5536P, Cell Signaling Technology), and anti‐mTOR (1:1000, 2893P, Cell Signaling Technology), anti‐PI3 Kinase (1:500, 9242, Cell Signaling Technology), and anti‐Phospho‐PI3 Kinase p85 (1:500, 19366S, Cell Signaling Technology) at 4°C. After washing with TBST, the membranes were incubated with corresponding HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies (1:10,000, Proteintech) at room temperature for 1 h. Protein bands were visualized using Chemiluminescent HRP Substrate (WBKLS0500, Millipore), and Image Lab 4.1 software (Bio‐Rad) was used for protein band quantification.

### Enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)

TNF‐α, IL‐10 in the supernatant of microglia were measured by ELISA kit (Multi Sciences) following the manufacturer's instructions.

### Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)

For TEM examination, spinal cord specimens underwent a specialized preparation procedure. Mice were euthanized with isoflurane and transcardially perfused with PBS and 4% paraformaldehyde solution. Subsequently, the spinal cord columns were isolated and consecutively fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde for 2 h, followed by 1% OsO4 for 45 min. Following fixation, samples were dehydrated using a gradient of ethanol (30%–100%) and embedded in Araldite resin. Sections (1 μm) were stained with toluidine blue, while ultrathin sections (60 nm) were cut using copper grids and stained with uranyl acetate (3%) and lead citrate (1%). TEM was performed using a transmission electron microscope (H‐7650, Hitachi) at an accelerating voltage of 100 kV.

### Basso Mouse Scale (BMS)

Hindlimb motor function was assessed using the BMS prior to surgery and on postoperative days 1, 3, 7, 14, and 28. The BMS scoring system assigns a score ranging from 0 to 9, where a score of 0 denotes no ankle movement and a score of 9 represents complete functional recovery. Two independent researchers conducted the observation and recording of hindlimb movements of animals.

### Louisville Swim Scale (LSS)

Hindlimb function, trunk instability, and body angle were assessed using the LSS prior to injury and at 3, 7, 14, and 28 days post‐SCI. The LSS assigns a score ranging from 0 to 17, where 0 indicates no hindlimb movement, and 17 indicates normal hindlimb movement. Each mouse was pre‐trained to swim. Two independent researchers recorded the average score of each mouse.

### Rotarod test

A rotarod apparatus equipped with an acceleration setting (ranging from 0 to 40 rpm) was used to evaluate gross motor function and coordination in mice. Each mouse underwent one practice trial, followed by two test trials, with a 20 min interval between trials. The average latency to fall from the rotarod was calculated based on the results of the two test trials for each animal.

### Statistical analysis

All data analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.0. For normality and lognormality tests, a Shapiro–Wilk was performed. For the comparison between groups, statistical significance was determined using the unpaired two‐tailed Student's t‐test. For multiple comparisons, a one‐way ANOVA with Fisher LSD test or Dunnett's multiple comparisons test for pairwise comparisons in multiple groups (for variables with homogenous variance) or Games–Howell (for variables with non‐homogenous variance), or two‐way ANOVA, followed by Tukey's multiple comparisons, was performed. Data are presented as the mean ± S.E.M. for at least three independent biological replicates. The “n” numbers for each experiment are specified in the figure legends. The three‐dimensional surface plot was generated with the ImageJ 1.52v. A value of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## RESULTS

### Fuc promotes locomotor function after SCI

To ascertain whether Fuc confers protective effects against SCI, we conducted animal experiments, as illustrated in Figure 1A, and assessed the motor function of mice. In short, Fuc is administered by i.p injection from day 1 to day 28 after SCI. Mice in the sham group only underwent spinal cord exposure without subsequent steps of injury; they were considered to be free of behavioral and histochemical staining defects and were only present as a positive reference group in TEM. In addition to histochemistry and TEM on day 7 and day 28 after SCI, both the vehicle group and the Fuc treatment groups underwent behavioral tests on the dates indicated in the experimental procedure.

The motor behavior of SCI mice was initially assessed using the BMS score. As shown in Figure 1F, all mice that underwent injury exhibited complete hindlimb paralysis (BMS score = 0) on day 1 after SCI, indicating successful and homogeneous modeling. Beginning at 3 days post injury(dpi), the animals demonstrated gradual, time‐dependent recovery, with varying degrees of improvement observed in all groups. Compared to the vehicle group, mice treated with Fuc demonstrated a trend toward higher BMS score elevation at 3–28 dpi, suggesting that Fuc treatment significantly promotes locomotor recovery. The results of the experiment showed BMS scores were significantly higher in the SCI + Fuc (10 mg, 20 mg/kg) group compared to the vehicle group (7, 14, and 28 dpi).

Swimming exactly reflects the motor capacity of the animal's nervous system. Hence, we performed swimming tests at multiple time points after SCI and used the LSS for quantitative assessment 21 (Figure 1C,D). As shown in Figure 1D, the motor function of all groups gradually recovered from day 7 after SCI, and the recovery rate was significantly faster in the Fuc‐treated groups, especially in the 20 mg/kg group.

In the rotarod test performed on day 28 after SCI, the Fuc‐treated groups demonstrated better balance and motor coordination on all tests compared to the vehicle group (Figure 1E). Taken together, these results indicated that Fuc treatment notably improved the motor function of SCI mice.

### Fuc reduces early inflammatory response after SCI and regulates microglial/macrophages polarization

Inflammation represents a pivotal target for SCI treatment, as its regulation can mitigate a spectrum of secondary damages and improve the injury microenvironment. 22 , 23 In our study, we used Iba1 as the marker to characterize microglia and macrophages, employing iNOS as a marker for M1‐type inflammatory cells and Arg1 as a marker for M2‐type ones. 24 Our findings (Figure 2A,C) distinctly illustrate that Fuc intervention significantly restricted the inflammatory extent within the injury site, concomitant with a marked reduction in inflammatory cell numbers. Correspondingly, the levels of iNOS and ARG1 proteins assessed by Western blotting were significantly higher in SCI lesions. Fuc treatment decreased the expression of iNOS while concurrently increasing that of ARG1 (Figure 2B,D). Furthermore, Fuc not only curbed inflammation but also reversed the polarization of inflammatory cells (Figure 2E–H). We also detected the levels of pro‐inflammatory cytokine (TNF‐α) and anti‐inflammatory cytokine (IL‐10) in the supernatant of microglia stimulated by LPS for 1 day using ELISA. After Fuc treatment, especially high‐dose Fuc treatment, the level of TNF‐α significantly decreased while the level of IL‐10 significantly increased (Figure S2). As aforementioned, this suggests that Fuc not only confines inflammation spread and diminishes injury scope but also transitions inflammatory cells from a pro‐inflammatory to an anti‐inflammatory, pro‐repair state.

### Fuc promotes neuronal survival and suppresses apoptosis after SCI

Following SCI, the survival of neurons at the injury site directly influences motor and sensory functions in mice. 25 To understand the anatomical basis of functional recovery in the treatment group, we conducted NeuN staining to identify surviving neurons and quantified the number of NeuN+ cells at various distances from the injury center in coronal slices across different experimental groups. In the Z1–Z3 region, the number of surviving neurons in the Fuc‐treated groups was significantly higher than in the vehicle group, with the neuroprotective effect of the Fuc 20 mg/kg group being superior to that of the Fuc 10 mg/kg group (Figure 3A,B). To further investigate the benefits of Fuc in SCI repair, primary cortical neurons were treated with H2O2 (100 μM) for 24 h to mimic neuronal injury. In the in vitro neuronal injury model, Fuc significantly enhanced neuronal survival, with higher concentrations exhibiting greater protective effects (Figure S1A–C).

### Fuc alleviates glial scar formation and promotes axonal regeneration following SCI

The primary manifestation of neurological dysfunction following SCI is the disruption of neural pathways, with axons serving as fundamental conduits for nerve impulse transmission. 27 Therefore, assessing axonal repair is crucial in evaluating SCI treatments. While astrocytic scars are thought to limit inflammation and protect nerve cells in the early stages of SCI, they subsequently impede axonal regeneration and extension, posing a significant obstacle to spinal cord repair. 28 To investigate neural repair post‐SCI in our study, we used GFAP as an astrocyte activation marker and NF200 to characterize neural axons. As depicted in Figure 4A–E, astrocytes proliferate and accumulate at the injury edge, forming a glial scar area post‐injury. Compared to the vehicle group, scar density significantly decreased in both treatment groups, with the high‐dose group (Fuc 20 mg/kg) demonstrating the most pronounced effect. Consistent with this finding, there was a significant increase in the number of axons within the injury area in the treatment groups, particularly in the Fuc 20 mg/kg group.

### Fuc promotes myelination after SCI

To evaluate the regeneration of myelin in the lesion region, we used NF‐200 to label axons 32 and MBP to label myelin sheaths. 33 Due to the observation of more axons and stronger OPC differentiation in the Fuc treatment groups than in the vehicle group, we further examined myelination in the injury area. As shown in the immunofluorescence double staining for MBP and NF200 (Figure 5E), there were more MBP+ and NF200+ signals in the Fuc treatment groups (Figure 5F,G), indicating an enhancement in myelination along with the increase in axon numbers compared to the vehicle group.

To accurately evaluate the remyelination efficiency, we performed TEM to distinguish unambiguously the normal myelin and pathological myelin within the lesion region. Considering the published studies 34 , 35 and our own experimental observations, in this work, we established five pathological grades of the myelin sheath ultrastructure in the lesion region (Figure 6C) (Data S1). Compared to the sham group, both the SCI + Veh and SCI + Fuc (20 mg/kg) groups showed varying degrees of demyelination. However, Fuc treatment resulted in extensive remyelination, as evidenced by improved pathological grade of myelin and by the emergence of abundant newly formed thin myelin sheaths (Figure 6A). Subsequently, TEM analysis of all groups revealed a higher proportion of myelinated axons in the SCI + Fuc group (Figure 6B). Notably, compared to the SCI + Veh group, the quantification of myelin pathology level uncovered a higher proportion of normal myelin/abnormal lamellae and a lower proportion of inclusions/outfoldings/myelin whorls in the lesions of the SCI + Fuc group at 28 dpi (Figure 6C,D). Taken together, these results demonstrate that Fuc treatment enhances the number of axons in the injury area and strengthens the myelin sheath structure of axons.

### Fuc promotes OPCs differentiation by activating the mTOR signaling pathway

Previous studies have shown that both the PI3K/AKT/mTOR and Ras/Raf/Mek/Erk pathways play important roles in the development of the OL lineage. 36 , 37 , 38 In order to reveal the pathways targeted by Fuc, we assessed the MBP expression in OPCs cultured in vitro and treated with Fuc plus different inhibitors. Western blotting analysis showed the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin notably blocked the increase of MBP expression in the 100 ng/mL group, whereas the MEK inhibitor U0126 had no blocking effect (Figure 8A,B). Furthermore, the increased MBP+/Hoechst+ cells with Fuc treatment were diminished after rapamycin was added (Figure 8C,D). In addition, Western blotting analysis showed that the addition of Fuc alone resulted in increased levels of p‐mTOR, whereas the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin inhibited the pro‐differentiation effect of Fuc (Figure 8C–E,G). To further confirm that the differentiation‐promoting effect of Fuc is mediated by the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, we co‐incubated OPCs with Wortmannin and LY294002, which are specific inhibitors for PI3K, an upstream molecule in the AKT/mTOR pathway (Figure 8F), Western blotting analysis showed that both inhibitors of PI3K reduced the phosphorylation level of mTOR to the control level (Figure 8H). These results indicate that Fuc modulates mTOR phosphorylation levels through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, thereby promoting the differentiation of OPCs.

## DISCUSSION

SCI remains a significant challenge due to its complex pathological basis, primarily characterized by inflammation cascades and the establishment of inhibitory spinal cord microenvironments. 22 The inflammatory response triggered by SCI involves the activation of immune cells and the release of pro‐inflammatory mediators, which not only exacerbates tissue damage but also disrupts the normal functioning of neurons. The activation of astrocytes has dual effects; while it protects neurons, its excessive activation leads to the formation of glial scars, which in turn creates an inhibitory microenvironment that hinders spinal cord repair. 39 Additionally, SCI induces widespread apoptosis of neurons, further compromising the structural and functional integrity of the spinal cord. 40 Moreover, the disruption of myelin sheaths, essential for nerve impulse conduction, is a hallmark of SCI. 41 Despite the potential for remyelination post‐SCI, its efficacy and pace lag significantly behind the extent of neuronal damage. This intricate interplay of pathological processes poses formidable hurdles for effective SCI treatment strategies. In this study, we demonstrated that the innovative intervention by Fuc mitigates the detrimental effects of SCI and improves functional recovery in mice. In the SCI model, Fuc inhibits inflammation and reverses inflammation polarization, reduces the formation of reactive astrocyte scars, alleviates apoptosis, and promotes remyelination processes.

Following SCI, inflammation is an important defense mechanism against harmful stimuli, but the inflammatory cascade and the sustained and exacerbated inflammation reaction exacerbate nerve damage. 42 Seeking effective interventions for the inflammatory cascade has been a focus of SCI research. 43 Fuc, a sulfated polysaccharide rich in L‐fucose, is commonly found in brown algae and sea cucumbers. 44 It is a non‐toxic polysaccharide with diverse biological functions. 13 Multiple studies have confirmed the broad anti‐inflammatory effects of fucoidan, 45 , 46 , 47 and in recent years, its neuroprotective effects have been demonstrated. 18 , 19 After SCI, resident microglia are rapidly activated, whereas peripheral macrophages infiltrate the injury site several hours later in response to inflammatory chemokines, together constituting the main inflammatory cells involved in the inflammatory response. Microglia and macrophages are classified into classical M1 and M2 types based on the differences in the inflammatory factors they secrete, with M1 typically exhibiting pro‐inflammatory characteristics and M2 exhibiting anti‐inflammatory characteristics, leading to different inflammatory outcomes. 48 This study confirms that during the first week after injury, which is when the commonly recognized peak of inflammation occurs, Fuc significantly restricts the spread of inflammation and reverses the polarization of inflammation. According to previous studies, this anti‐inflammatory effect is likely to improve neuron survival, alleviate apoptosis, and improve the post‐injury microenvironment.

Apoptosis is a significant mode of cell death for neurons in SCI. The survival of neurons is particularly fundamental for the repair process post‐SCI, and suppressing neuronal apoptosis holds critical significance for SCI treatment. 49 Apoptosis is regulated by multiple factors, including primary injury, inflammation, oxidative stress, and levels of apoptosis‐related proteins. 50 Our findings confirm a significant increase in the number of surviving neurons in the injured area following Fuc application, coupled with a notable reduction in neuronal apoptosis. Therefore, we posit that Fuc not only inhibits inflammation but also alleviates neuronal apoptosis, ultimately leading to a remarkable increase in the number of neurons, thus providing greater potential for subsequent neural function restoration.

After SCI occurs, astrocytes promptly undergo activation, contributing to glial scar development at the injury site as part of the reparative process. 39 Activated astrocytes release a variety of cytokines, including inflammatory mediators and growth factors, which are pivotal in the healing and regenerative mechanisms following injury. 51 Excessive astrocyte activation can lead to scar formation and the establishment of an inhibitory microenvironment, impeding neuronal regeneration and repair. 52 Hence, modulation of astrocyte biology represents a promising avenue for the treatment of SCI. Our results demonstrate that Fuc exhibits a dose‐dependent effect in inhibiting astrocyte activation and reducing glial scar formation while also enhancing the density of axons at the injury site, thus providing a favorable foundation for functional recovery.

The recovery of motor function post‐SCI relies significantly on the regeneration of myelin sheaths, provided that axonal regeneration efficiency is moderately ensured. Typically, myelin regeneration hinges on the differentiation and maturation of OPCs. 53 Following demyelination, OPCs swiftly transition from a quiescent state to an activated state, subsequently undergoing recruitment, proliferation, and differentiation into mature OLs. These mature OLs then generate new myelin sheaths, safeguarding axons and restoring signaling integrity. 54 , 55

In our in vivo experiments, immunofluorescence staining revealed an increased population of SOX10+ cells within the lesion site after Fuc treatment compared to the control group, indicating that Fuc intervention promoted the survival of OLs lineage. Here, we speculate that this effect may be associated with the anti‐inflammatory and anti‐apoptotic actions of Fuc. Concurrently, under the intervention of Fuc at two different doses, the quantity of CC1+ cells increased. Moreover, comparing the two treatment groups, the 20 mg/kg Fuc group exhibited a higher proportion of CC1+ cells among SOX10+ cells. This facilitation of OPCs differentiation was further visualized through the increased number of MBP‐positive axons, and TEM analysis. These collective findings confirm that intervention with Fuc can enhance the survival of OPCs post‐SCI and promote their differentiation and maturation. Existing evidence establishes the anti‐inflammatory, antioxidant, and neuroprotective effects of Fuc in neurological diseases. 16 However, its role in promoting OPCs differentiation remains unexplored. Therefore, our studies focused on investigating the impact of Fuc on OPCs differentiation through in vitro experiments.

To further investigate whether Fuc has a differentiation‐promoting effect on OPCs, we conducted additional in vitro experiments. The experimental findings validated that Fuc treatment notably enhanced OPCs differentiation without impacting their proliferation and apoptosis. Eventually, this promotion of differentiation is anticipated to facilitate effective myelin regeneration.

The Ras/Raf/Mek/Erk pathway has been reported to play an important role in the progression of the OLs spectrum. 38 , 56 However, our results indicated that an inhibitor of MEK upstream of ERK (U0126) did not block the Fuc‐induced differentiation‐promoting effects of OPCs, suggesting that these effects are independent of the ERK1/2 pathway.

Previous reports indicated that Fuc regulates metabolism through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis. 57 , 58 AKT, a serine/threonine kinase in the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, plays a crucial role in regulating cell survival, proliferation, angiogenesis, and metabolism. 59 Phosphorylated AKT (p‐AKT) directly activates the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) by phosphorylating the Ser2448 site of mTORC1. 60 mTOR is a downstream effector of AKT signaling, which is quite critical for OPCs differentiation and myelin formation. 61 Rapamycin is an mTOR inhibitor that inhibits the differentiation of OPCs and the expression of most myelin proteins. 38 Our experimental results show that Fuc increases the phosphorylation level of mTOR, which can be blocked by rapamycin. Thus, Fuc‐induced OPCs differentiation may be mediated primarily through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway.

Activation of mTOR signals may also regulate the pathology of SCI via anti‐inflammatory and anti‐apoptotic effects. It is reported that fucoidan can alleviate H2O2‐induced neuronal apoptosis and exert neuroprotective effects by activating the PI3K/AKT pathway, 62 while medications that promote the AKT/mTOR signaling can alleviate neuronal apoptosis induced by vascular dementia 63 or traumatic brain injury. 64 In addition, blocking the activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway with PI3K inhibitor not only exacerbates cell apoptosis, but also increases the expression of neuroinflammatory factors TNF‐α and IL‐1β, 65 while mTOR inhibitor can promote the activation of NF‐κB signaling and increase the production of pro‐inflammatory factors such as IL‐1β and IL‐6 in human monocytes. 66 These results indicate that fucoidan may play an important role in SCI by activating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, reducing inflammatory response and neuronal apoptosis. However, due to the complexity of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, its exact role in SCI still needs further investigation.

Based on this experimental study, we hypothesized that Fuc would be an effective drug for the treatment of SCI because it could potentially inhibit inflammation, reduce neuronal apoptosis, improve the regeneration of spinal cord‐injured axons, and promote their myelination. Moreover, we found for the first time that Fuc specifically promotes the differentiation and maturation of OPCs through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. The findings provide a potential strategy for SCI treatment.

Although the effects of Fuc on neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and neuronal survival in several neurological diseases have been documented, its unique role in SCI remains unexplored. Thus, more detailed studies are needed to enhance our understanding on the roles and mechanisms of Fuc in SCI. In addition, it is crucial of continued in‐depth research on metabolism and distribution characteristics of Fuc in SCI for determining the appropriate therapeutic dosage and duration.

# Abstract

Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) faces significant challenges in modernization and integration into Western healthcare systems due to fundamental differences in diagnostic approaches, treatment targets, and underlying philosophies. Direct application of Western methodologies to TCM proves inadequate, necessitating a tailored approach that respects TCM’s unique aspects while ensuring scientific rigor. This article examines the challenges and opportunities in modernizing TCM, with a focus on its integration into Western healthcare systems governed by stringent regulatory frameworks such as those of the Food and Drug Administration in the US. It explores innovative strategies, such as using composite hypotheses in clinical trials to align evaluation criteria with TCM’s holistic approach and strategically using real-world data and evidence to enhance regulatory submissions. The proposed methodologies offer novel ways to bridge the divide between TCM and Western medicine, potentially transforming policy and practice in global healthcare systems. By adopting an approach that respects the unique aspects of TCM while ensuring scientific rigor, successful integration into Western health-care systems could be achieved, leveraging TCM’s potential benefits for patient care.

## 1. Introduction

## 2. Fundamental differences between WM and TCM

For the modernization of TCM clinical development, one may consider applying well-established Western processes

directly to the TCM. However, this Westernization process may not be feasible due to some fundamental differences between WM and TCM, which are summarized in Table 1. These fundamental differences are briefly described below:

### 2.1. Principal ingredients and dosage flexibility

One of the most striking differences between WM and TCM lies in their approach to medicinal ingredients and dosage. WM typically focuses on a singular active ingredient, with standardized dosages for each patient. In contrast, TCM often employs a combination of several ingredients, tailoring the dosage according to individual needs. This personalized approach allows TCM practitioners to address the unique constitution and specific imbalances of each patient.7

### 2.2. Diagnostic approach and outcome measures

WM relies on empirical evidence and validated diagnostic tools, focusing on established clinical outcomes and objective measures such as imaging, blood tests, and standardized protocols to assess a patient’s condition.8 This approach is grounded in identifying specific pathophysiological processes, emphasizing quantifiable data to guide diagnosis and treatment.

In contrast, TCM is rooted in ancient theories like Yin and Yang, which represent the dualistic nature of all things – Yin being the passive, cooling, and nurturing aspect, and Yang being the active, warming, and driving force.9 These concepts, along with the theory of Qi (vital energy), form the foundation of TCM diagnosis. Qi is considered the life force that flows through the body, and its balance and harmony are essential for health.10 TCM practitioners assess the balance of Yin and Yang and the flow of Qi through observations and the patient’s subjective experiences, such as their emotional state and overall wellbeing. Instead of relying on standardized measures, TCM evaluates treatment effectiveness through improvements in Qi balance, the restoration of harmony between Yin and Yang, and the alleviation of symptoms as perceived by the patient. This holistic approach often involves practices such as acupuncture, herbal medicine, and Qigong, aiming to harmonize the body’s internal energies with the surrounding forces of heaven and earth.10

### 2.3. Therapeutic target and foundation

While WM aims to target specific organs or systems affected by a disease, TCM focuses on restoring overall body harmony and balance.7 This difference in therapeutic targets stems from the distinct foundations of each medical system. WM is grounded in empirical evidence and scientific research, constantly evolving as new discoveries are made. In contrast, TCM draws

### 2.4. Analysis perspective and approach to medicine

WM adopts a population-based analysis perspective, emphasizing the generalizability of treatment outcomes across large groups of patients. This approach aligns with the principles of precision medicine, which aims to minimize intersubjective variability by developing targeted therapies based on an individual’s genetic profile and other biomarkers.11 Conversely, TCM takes an individual-centric approach, emphasizing the customization of treatment plans to address the unique needs of each patient. This aligns with the principles of personalized medicine, which seeks to minimize intrasubject variability by tailoring treatments to the individual’s specific constitution and imbalances.7

## 3. Westernization of TCM

The integration of TCM into the Western healthcare system has been significantly influenced by the regulatory frameworks established by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the US (US). The FDA’s approach to botanical and biologically based TCM products – categorized based on their intended use as drugs, dietary supplements, or foods – reflects a broader global trend toward the acceptance and standardization of complementary and alternative medicines (CAM).12

In 2004, the FDA addressed the increasing incorporation of CAM, including TCM, into the US health-care market.13 The guidelines established aimed to ensure that TCM products intended for use as drugs met safety and efficacy standards comparable to those for conventional pharmaceuticals. This required applying Western clinical research methodologies to demonstrate the safety and effectiveness of TCM products – a challenging task due to the complex mixtures and individualized treatment

approaches inherent to TCM. The 2004 guidelines marked a significant step toward clarifying the regulatory landscape for CAM products, emphasizing the need for scientific validation within a framework traditionally oriented toward synthetic, single-agent pharmaceuticals.

The progression toward the 2016 regulations highlighted the FDA’s commitment to adapting its regulatory framework to better accommodate the unique aspects of TCM.12 The updated guidelines provided more explicit guidance on the pre-market evaluation process for botanical drugs, facilitating the integration of TCM products into the US health-care system.12 These regulations underscored the importance of rigorous clinical trials, quality control, and manufacturing standards while also addressing the challenge of standardizing TCM formulations. The 2016 guidelines represented a nuanced approach to TCM regulation, acknowledging the need for a balance between ensuring public safety and preserving the traditional practices and philosophies that define TCM.

The FDA’s regulatory frameworks for TCM have played a crucial role in its Westernization, enabling TCM products to gain legitimacy and acceptance within the Western medical community. However, the adaptation of TCM to meet Western scientific and regulatory standards has also sparked concerns about the potential erosion of traditional knowledge and methodologies. The focus on scientific validation and the standardization of TCM formulations may not fully capture the holistic and individualized nature of TCM practices.

For instance, the demand for evidence-based outcomes through clinical trials may not always align with TCM’s individualized treatment approach, which is based on personalized diagnoses and natural, complex herbal formulations rather than single, isolated active ingredients. In addiion, the financial and logistical challenges associated with conducting Western-style clinical trials pose significant barriers to TCM practitioners and researchers,

## 4. Modernization of TCM development

Given the limitations of applying traditional Western pharmaceutical development processes to TCM, an alternative approach is to consider the modernization of TCM development. This approach aims to be a scientifically objective, evidence-based method that respects the unique characteristics of TCM while ensuring the safety and efficacy of TCM products. In the modernization of TCM development, several key aspects must be considered from both clinical and regulatory perspectives:

### 4.1. Clinical investigation

In the development of WMs, the traditional Western approach is to power the study based on the efficacy endpoint alone. The WM will be approved if the null hypothesis of ineffectiveness is rejected and there appears to be no evidence of safety concerns. This approach has been criticized because the clinical study is powered based on the efficacy endpoint alone, which targets specific organs but does not account for safety concerns that may be induced by other organs. As a result, many drug products were withdrawn due to safety concerns after regulatory approval. A typical example is the withdrawal of Vioxx (intended for pain relief), which was approved by the FDA in 1999 but was withdrawn in 2004 due to a high risk of heart attack and stroke.14

TCM takes a holistic approach to healthcare, aiming to restore and maintain the overall balance and harmony of the body’s systems, in contrast to WM, which typically focuses on targeting specific organs or systems affected by a disease. Given these philosophical differences, modernizing the development of TCM should involve testing composite hypotheses that consider both safety and efficacy in clinical investigations, as proposed by Chow and Shao15 (Table 2). When assessing the efficacy of a treatment, researchers commonly employ tests for superiority (S), non-inferiority (N), or therapeutic equivalence (E) hypotheses, which compare the performance of the new treatment to an existing control or standard of care.

Similarly, for safety assessment, investigators analyze the safety profile of the treatment, including adverse events and other relevant parameters, to determine whether the test treatment is superior, non-inferior, or equivalent to the control in terms of safety. By incorporating both safety and efficacy considerations into composite hypotheses, researchers can develop a more comprehensive approach to evaluating TCM treatments, acknowledging the unique characteristics of TCM while ensuring that the treatments meet modern standards for safety and effectiveness.

It should be noted that achieving statistical significance with the desired power for correctly detecting clinically meaningful differences in both safety and efficacy parameters (endpoints) in clinical trials will require a much larger sample size. To overcome this problem, some out-of-the-box innovative thinking is necessary, which will be further discussed in a later section of this article.

### 4.2. Establishment of standards for TCM

As the traditional subjective experience-based assessment, regardless of the sufficient documentation, is not convincing and hence not acceptable for providing substantial evidence in support of regulatory submissions of TCMs, the modernization of TCM development requires a set of standards for diagnostic procedures, evaluation, and regulatory review for an accurate and reliable assessment of the safety and efficacy of TCM under development scientifically. The standards for diagnostic procedures, evaluation, and regulatory review can help in providing objective and substantial evidence for the evaluation of the safety and efficacy of the TCMs under investigation. Unlike WMs, currently, there are no universally accepted objective standards for diagnostic and evaluation procedures for TCMs across different therapeutic areas.16

### 4.3. Validation against western standards

Since there are no universally accepted objective diagnostic and evaluation procedures for TCMs, the development and validation of tools such as quality-oflife-like instruments is necessary. For the validation of the developed instruments, it is suggested that the validation be performed against well-established Western standards

### 4.4. Examples of current TCM modernization efforts

Recent efforts to modernize TCM have resulted in significant advancements that bridge traditional practices with modern scientific approaches. One notable example is the clinical research on carotid artery plaque intervention with the Tongxinluo capsule. This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, led by Zhang et al.,17 involved 1212  patients with carotid atherosclerotic plaque. The study demonstrated that Tongxinluo therapy, when added to conventional treatment, could slow the progression of carotid intimamedia thickness, plaque area, and vascular remodeling index, while also reducing cardiovascular events with a strong safety profile.

Another example is the global success of artemisinin, a compound derived from the TCM herb Artemisia annua.18 Discovered by Tu Youyou, artemisinin has become a firstline treatment for malaria, endorsed by the WHO. Its widespread use has contributed significantly to malaria control, including near eradication in regions such as the Comoros Islands, and earned Tu the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2015.19

In addition, galantamine, extracted from the TCM herb Lycoris radiata, is now an approved treatment for Alzheimer’s disease in Europe. As an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, galantamine’s success showcases the potential of TCM-derived compounds in treating complex neurological conditions.20

Despite the successes, it is essential to note that while compounds such as artemisinin and galantamine, derived from TCM herbs, have achieved global recognition and widespread use; their development involved simplifying the complex formulations typical of TCM into single compounds. These examples still reflect a degree of Westernization, as the process of isolating active compounds from TCM herbs tends to align more with Western pharmaceutical practices than with traditional TCM approaches. Therefore, while these examples highlight the success of integrating TCM into modern medicine, they also underscore the ongoing need for TCM modernization that remains true to its holistic and multi-component nature. The challenge lies in preserving the complexity and synergy inherent in traditional formulations while ensuring that they meet the rigorous standards of modern clinical practice.

## 5. Innovative thinking on the modernization of TCM development

In the pursuit of modernizing TCM development, several innovative approaches from other fields can be adapted to enhance TCM clinical trials. These approaches include: (i) demonstrating “not unsafe” for safety and “not ineffectiveness” for efficacy; (ii) using composite hypotheses to evaluate both safety and efficacy simultaneously; and (iii) incorporating RWD and RWE to support regulatory approval. These innovative approaches will be briefly described below.

### 5.1. The concept of demonstrating not unsafe and not ineffectiveness

The concept of demonstrating “not unsafe” and “not ineffectiveness” differs from the conventional approach of demonstrating “safe” and “effective.” In this approach, the null hypothesis of ineffectiveness is tested against the alternative hypothesis of “not ineffectiveness” rather than “effectiveness”.21 Rejecting the null hypothesis in favor of “not ineffectiveness” does not necessarily imply effectiveness. This approach can be particularly useful in TCM development as well as in the development of drugs for rare diseases.21

In practice, researchers typically test the null hypothesis at the α = 5% level of significance, although some prefer testing at the α = 1% level. If the observed P-value falls between 1% and 5%, the test result is considered inconclusive. In placebo-controlled studies, “not ineffectiveness” conceptually includes both the portion of inconclusiveness and effectiveness (Figure 1).

Applying this approach to TCM clinical trials can provide a more nuanced understanding of the efficacy of TCM treatments. By demonstrating “not ineffectiveness,” researchers can show that a TCM treatment has the potential to be effective, even if the evidence is not strong enough to claim definitive effectiveness. This approach can be particularly valuable in the context of TCM, where the

### 5.2. Composite hypothesis for safety and efficacy

As discussed in Section 3, the Western approach – powering the intended clinical trial based on efficacy endpoint alone – for evaluating the safety and efficacy of WMs under development may not be appropriate regardless of whether WMs target specific organs. Unlike WMs, it is suggested that the modernization of TCM, which focuses on global dynamic balance/harmony among organs, should consider testing composite hypotheses of safety and efficacy at the same time. However, this approach often requires a larger sample size to achieve statistical significance and detect clinically meaningful differences or safety concerns. To address this challenge, an innovative approach based on probability statements can be employed for sample size justification.

For example, in a TCM clinical trial, the composite hypotheses could be set up as follows: (i)	 Null hypothesis: The TCM is ineffective and unsafe (ii)	 Alternative hypothesis: The TCM is not ineffective

and not unsafe.

By testing these hypotheses with a reasonable number of subjects, researchers can assess the safety and efficacy of the TCM under investigation. If the null hypothesis is rejected, it indicates that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the treatment is “not unsafe” and “not ineffective.”

This approach allows a more comprehensive evaluation of TCM treatments by considering both safety and efficacy aspects. Using composite hypotheses allows researchers to better align their statistical methods with the holistic nature of TCM, which emphasizes the importance of balance and harmony within the body. In addition, this approach can streamline the clinical trial process for TCM treatments by enabling the concurrent assessment of safety and efficacy, potentially reducing the need for separate trials.

### 5.3. The use of real-world design/RWE in support of regulatory submission

Expanding on the concept introduced in the previous section, Chow suggested a novel two-step approach for evaluating the efficacy of a test drug. The first step involves testing for “not-ineffectiveness” (N), followed by testing for effectiveness (S) once the not-ineffectiveness of the test drug has been established.21 This approach is applicable when the probability of inconclusiveness has little or no clinical significance and can be considered negligible. To rule out the probability of inconclusiveness, Chow proposed utilizing data from the intended randomized clinical trial

in combination with RWD and RWE to support regulatory submissions.21 Although initially proposed for rare disease drug development, this innovative approach can also be applied to TCM development, particularly when the sample size required to demonstrate safety is not feasible within the intended RCT. It should be noted that the use of RWD/RWE in support of TCM regulatory submissions is scientifically valid only under the assumption that RWD is representative of the target patient population under study. Thus, a pre-study evaluation of the RWD in terms of its representativeness, bias, consistency, data quality, and relevance is strongly recommended.

### 5.4. TCM clinical trial design

Designing clinical trials for TCM that accurately reflect its unique diagnostic and therapeutic approaches is essential for integrating TCM into global health-care practices. A  well-fitted clinical trial design for TCM, such as the one described by Fu and Chow, offers a comprehensive structure that bridges the methodologies of WM and TCM.22

In this design, subjects are initially randomized into two groups. One group undergoes screening using established Western study endpoints, while the other is screened through Chinese diagnostic procedures. Following screening, eligible participants in each group are further randomized to receive either a test treatment (T) or a control (C). This secondary stratification creates four distinct subgroups, each receiving an evaluation either in the Western manner or according to Chinese methods. Figure  2 provides a visual illustration of the design.

The primary advantage of this design is its ability to provide a robust comparative analysis of TCM and WM treatment effects within the same study framework. By evaluating the treatment effects using both Western and Chinese diagnostic and evaluation methods, the study design allows for a nuanced understanding of how TCM treatments perform under different evaluative lenses. This dual approach facilitates a more comprehensive evaluation of TCM’s efficacy, potentially uncovering benefits or effects that might be overlooked if only traditional Western methodologies were employed.

Furthermore, this design enables the examination of the consistency between Western and Chinese evaluation methods across the subgroups. Such an analysis can reveal how TCM treatments’ efficacy might be perceived differently through the paradigms of Western and Chinese medicine, offering insights into the comparative validity and reliability of outcome measures across these medical systems.

## 6. Practical/challenging issues in TCM modernization

For the modernization of TCM clinical development, clinical trials evaluating the safety and efficacy of the TCM under investigation must be conducted under a valid study design. When conducting TCM clinical trials, practitioners inevitably encounter several practical and challenging issues, which are briefly outlined below.

### 6.1. Preparation of matching placebo

In TCM clinical trials, preparing a matching placebo is essential to maintain blinding integrity and minimize potential biases that may arise from knowledge of treatment assignment. Creating a quality-matching placebo that mirrors the test drug in physical form, sensory perception, packaging, and labeling, while having no pharmaceutical activity, is challenging but crucial.

Fai et al.23 developed a satisfactory placebo capsule that matched an herbal medicine in terms of its physical form, chemical nature, appearance, packaging, and labeling. They concluded that a matching placebo could be created for an RCT involving herbal medicine and discussed the means to acquire a patent for the developed placebo.

However, maintaining blinding integrity and avoiding operational biases due to knowledge of treatment assignments remains a major challenge. In TCM clinical trials, oral capsules are often used to prepare a matching placebo, as they can mask the strong smell and taste of herbal medicines. Nonetheless, there is a risk that patients

or clinicians might reveal treatment assignments if they break the capsules. To ensure the success of the blinding process, it is essential to establish standard operating procedures that prevent capsule breakage by both patients and clinicians.

### 6.2. Development of clinical endpoint

The selection of appropriate clinical endpoints is crucial in TCM clinical trials to accurately assess the safety and efficacy of the treatment under investigation. Unlike WM, which often relies on well-established and widely accepted clinical endpoints, TCM may require the development of novel endpoints that capture the holistic nature of the treatment and align with the principles of TCM theory.24 These endpoints should be clinically meaningful, reliable, and sensitive to treatment effects.

Collaboration between TCM practitioners and Western clinicians is essential to developing clinical endpoints that are both relevant to TCM and acceptable to the scientific community. This process should involve a thorough understanding of TCM principles and the specific condition being treated, as well as a critical evaluation of the existing endpoints used in WM. The developed endpoints should be validated in pilot studies to ensure their reliability and sensitivity before being implemented in large-scale clinical trials.

### 6.3. Development and validation of an instrument

To assess the safety and effectiveness of TCM treatments, it is often necessary to develop and validate quantitative instruments that can capture the complex and multifaceted nature of TCM outcomes.25 These instruments should be designed to measure relevant domains, such as symptom severity, quality of life, and overall well-being, in a manner that is consistent with TCM theory and practice.

The development process should involve a rigorous methodology, including item generation, pilot testing, and psychometric evaluation. Item generation should be based on a comprehensive review of TCM literature, expert opinion, and patient input to ensure that the instrument covers all relevant aspects of the condition being treated. Pilot testing should be conducted to assess the clarity, comprehensibility, and acceptability of the items, as well as to identify any potential issues with administration or scoring.26

Psychometric evaluation is critical to establishing the reliability and validity of the instrument. Reliability refers to the consistency and reproducibility of the instrument’s scores, while validity refers to the extent to which the instrument measures what it intends to measure. Various types of reliability (e.g., internal consistency, test-retest, inter-rater) and validity (e.g., content, construct, and criterion) should be assessed using appropriate statistical methods.27 The resulting instrument should demonstrate adequate psychometric properties to be considered a valid tool for use in TCM clinical trials.

### 6.4. Calibrating TCM diagnostics with Western standards

The integration of TCM into modern healthcare systems presents a unique challenge, particularly in the realm of diagnostics. While TCM practitioners rely on timehonored quantitative instruments to assess disease severity and treatment efficacy, these tools often face skepticism from Western clinicians due to their perceived subjectivity and lack of alignment with established clinical endpoints.28 To bridge this gap and foster the global acceptance of TCM, we proposed a novel approach: the

development of a standardized, cross-cultural diagnostic framework that aligns TCM assessments with Western clinical standards.29

This innovative framework would build on the existing TCM quantitative instrument, which rates disease severity on a scale from 0 to 100, and introduce a more granular, continuous scale that eliminates the broad categorization of disease states into quartiles (health, mild, moderate, and severe). By adopting a linear scale, the framework would allow for more precise differentiation between adjacent scores, thereby addressing the critical limitations of the current categorical approach.

To ensure the validity and reliability of this new diagnostic framework, it is recommended to conduct a rigorous calibration process involving multi-center, crosscultural clinical trials. During these trials, patients would be assessed using both the enhanced TCM instrument and gold-standard Western diagnostic tools. Statistical techniques, including structural equation modeling and machine learning algorithms, should be employed to uncover correlations and predictive relationships between TCM assessments and Western clinical outcomes.

The successful development of a standardized, crosscultural diagnostic framework has the potential to enhance the precision of TCM diagnostics and promote a common language between TCM practitioners and Western clinicians. This shared understanding could facilitate the exchange of knowledge, experiences, and best practices, potentially leading to the development of more effective and personalized treatment strategies that incorporate insights from both medical traditions.30

Moreover, the calibration of TCM diagnostics with Western clinical standards could support the integration of TCM into international disease classification systems, such as the ICD.3 This integration would further validate TCM as a complementary approach to WM, enabling healthcare providers worldwide to utilize the unique perspectives and therapeutic methods offered by TCM.

## 7. Conclusion

The modernization of TCM clinical development is a complex and multifaceted process that requires a delicate balance between preserving TCM’s unique characteristics and adopting rigorous scientific methods to evaluate its safety and efficacy. As discussed in this article, this process involves addressing fundamental differences between WM and TCM, developing innovative approaches to clinical trial design and analysis, and overcoming practical and methodological challenges encountered in TCM clinical trials.

The successful modernization of TCM clinical development has the potential to bring significant benefits to patients worldwide. By integrating TCM into modern healthcare systems, patients may gain access to safe, effective, and holistic treatment options that complement and enhance the current standard of care. Moreover, the modernization of TCM can contribute to the advancement of medical knowledge by fostering a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of TCM treatments and by identifying new avenues for drug discovery and development.

However, the modernization of TCM clinical development is not without its challenges. It requires a collaborative effort among TCM practitioners, Western clinicians, researchers, and regulatory authorities to establish standardized diagnostic procedures, evaluation methods, and regulatory frameworks that are acceptable to both TCM and Western medical communities. It also calls for a willingness to embrace innovative thinking and novel approaches to clinical trial design and analysis while maintaining the highest standards of scientific rigor and ethical conduct.

Looking ahead, the future of healthcare may increasingly involve the synergy of these two systems. TCM’s plantbased formulations could provide alternative or adjunctive therapies to synthetic drugs, potentially reducing side effects and improving patient outcomes. For instance, the combination of TCM’s multi-component therapies with the precision of WM could lead to more personalized and effective treatments.

However, achieving this integration will require ongoing research, validation, and collaboration between TCM practitioners, scientists, and regulatory bodies. The goal should be to preserve the unique characteristics of TCM while ensuring that its practices meet the rigorous safety and efficacy standards expected in modern medicine. This approach not only holds promise for enhancing patient care but also for expanding the therapeutic arsenal available to modern medicine.

The modernization of TCM clinical development represents a significant opportunity to harness the potential of this ancient healing tradition and to bring its benefits to patients in a safe, effective, and scientifically validated manner. By embracing the challenges and opportunities associated with this process, we can work toward a future in which TCM and WM are integrated seamlessly, providing patients with the best possible care and outcomes.
